This is a tale from a little while ago. Once upon a time, there was a girl who loved books very much. She went to her school library almost every day to borrow books, so everyone called her a “bookworm.” But one day, she suddenly and mysteriously disappeared. No one knew where she went, and rumors spread through the school that she had been spirited away. Strangely, however, the book she had borrowed at that time was found returned to the library’s shelves.
–Rules– Players take turns flipping over books laid out in a row, starting from one end. (This action is called “borrowing a book.”) The player who happens to borrow the book whose checkout record says “Bookworm” becomes the loser of the game. Use the various effects that the books possess, observe your opponent carefully, and aim for victory!

🎄 In Santa’s workshop, you must fulfill a wish list by exchanging, passing, or even stealing cards. Overview You are one of the helpers at Santa’s workshop and have been assigned to fulfill the wishlist of two children by exchanging, passing, or even stealing cards from other players. Be the first to complete both of your assignments and you win!
Components The North Pole contains 18 poker sized cards, that include into two types of cards: Assignment cards (4) and Present Cards (14). Assignment cards show your assigned wishlists, with one on each side. Each wish list has 3 items, Present cards have two parts: the present associated with a wishlist and a power to use during play.
Game Play: Draw cards from the draw or discard pile until you have 2 cards in your hand. Do one of the following: Play a card and resolve its power. Discard a card and draw a card from the draw pile. Pass and take no action. Check for completion of your assignment. If complete do the following: Reveal your present cards If you have the gift card, discard it. Return any remaining cards to your hand.

2018 version Awesome, abstract, tile-laying game - based around the powers of 2. Players take turns placing tiles by matching the symbols on the four corners of the tiles. Each time a tile is placed, tokens are placed on the newly placed tile and adjacent tiles. Tiles occupied by a player's tokens become their territory. In the end, player with the highest total score from their occupied tiles wins.
This puzzle game, titled “Heúrēkaⁿ”, involves strategic placement of tiles where the goal is to match numbers at the corners to score points. It’s designed to be both educational, by teaching players about powers of 2, and entertaining, suitable for both solo and multiplayer modes. The gameplay stimulates both logical thinking and creative problem-solving, making it a comprehensive brain exercise.
Get points by matching the numbers at the four corners of the tiles! You’ll naturally learn powers of 2 while playing! It’s a brain exercise that uses both your left and right hemispheres! Try to capture as much territory as possible on a 6×6 board while cornering your opponent! Play competitively or Enjoy the math puzzle to your heart’s content if you’re playing solo!

🇯🇵 JAPAN ボードゲーム ボスサリーノ(Bossarino) Bossarino, a 2-player hidden boss hide-and-seek board game by Q's Games where one player hides their boss among upside-down hats, and the other tries to find it by moving and challenging pieces. The game involves square grid movement, challenging opponents, and strategic placement of pieces, with a goal of either finding the hidden boss or helping your own boss escape.
Gameplay Overview Players: 2 players Objective: One player hides their "boss" under one of several upside-down hats or pieces, while the other player tries to locate it. Mechanics: Players take turns moving pieces on a square grid. Moves: Move a piece one space in any direction. Swap positions with an opponent's piece. Challenge an opposing piece, which presumably reveals whether it's the boss or not. Winning: The game ends when the hidden boss is found or the player successfully moves their boss off the board, depending on the specific game setup.
Game Details Publisher: Q's Games Designer: om (おむ) Artist: Kenichi Kunimoto, Tetsuya Nishimura Playtime: Approximately 3-7 minutes

Even though it’s right before quitting time, everyone keeps bringing you overtime work. It seems other people are being asked to work overtime as well. When you’re given multiple tasks by the same person or similar types of work, you can shove them off by saying, “While you’re at it, could you handle this too?” When the game ends, the player with the fewest tasks left in front of them wins.
The game features six characters: President, Executive Director, Department Manager, Section Chief, Senior Employee, and Temp Worker. These six characters assign four types of overtime work: Answering the Phone, Sorting Slips, Copying, and Warehouse Organizing.
Each player mixes all their tiles well with the character side (white background) facing up, without looking at the backs. Then they take one tile of each character and line them up in front of themselves. The back side of each tile shows which task that character has assigned.
On your turn, you may do only one of the following two actions: Flip a tile showing its character side to reveal the work side. Once a tile has been flipped to the work side, it can never be turned back. Stack one of your work-side tiles onto another work-side tile already in play. You may stack it either on a tile in front of you or on one in front of another player. You may stack tiles if the top tile of the stack shows the same character or the same type of work. Once tiles have been stacked together, if you later stack them onto something else, the whole stack moves as one. Again, stacks can only be combined if the top tiles match in character or job; lower tiles don’t matter.
The game ends when no one can flip a character tile or stack any tiles anymore. At that point, the player with the fewest tiles remaining in front of them wins. If you have none left at all, it means you get to go home without doing any overtime—so you happily declare, “Sorry, I’m heading out first!” The rules are simple and the game moves at a quick pace, but halfway through it suddenly turns into a game of looking ahead and planning. You’ll need to consider the intentions of the other players and think carefully about the best ways to move your tiles.
